doc.title: Howard Levy interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 11, 2025

title: Crescent, Elvin Jones and Roland Kirk, and arriving at Northwestern
summary: He describes WLIB radio, first hearing live jazz with Elvin Jones and Roland Kirk, his parents' tastes, and auditioning for the Northwestern jazz band.

venues.name: Museum of Modern Art sculpture garden

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Hell of a place to start.

Yeah. And my poor teenage brain was blown apart. Because I had been playing rock & roll and blues. But I hadn’t started playing harmonica yet. So I heard this and I just wore the record out. I just listened over and over again, like what are these guys doing, what is it. I learned, basically I could sing a lot of what I had listened to. I listened so many times that I could sing Coltrane’s solos without understanding like what they were or anything like that. And then I discovered – New York had a great – I grew up in New York – they had a great jazz radio station called WLIB and Billy Taylor was the program director. And they played all the greatest like Impulse! and Blue Note stuff and I’d write down the name of the album and I’d go to the record store and buy it. But then after I heard “Crescent” I said I want to hear these guys live but Coltrane had just passed away. And I looked around, I looked in the newspapers in New York like well what about those three other guys? Like I was just crazy about the whole thing. And I saw that Elvin was going to be playing a concert at the Museum of Modern Art sculpture garden. And so I got a few friends together and we went. So my first live jazz experience hearing jazz played live was Elvin and Roland Kirk playing together. So, you know –
I saw both those guys myself when I was like – in a way I was frightened.

Yeah. Yeah. I can understand that. I was just absolutely –you know it’s different if you’re in a more spacious venue but when you see – well anyway seeing Elvin, because I was trying to imagine like I’d only heard rock drumming, you know. And how – it sounds like

two guys and how is he doing that. And I just sat there with my jaw on the floor. I mean Elvin ruined me for hearing drummers. Any other drummer after that seemed like yeah, this guy’s pretty good but he ain’t Elvin. You know? And I went to hear Elvin as many times as I could after that. The trio with Joe Farrell and Jimmy Garrison, I got to hear that a bunch of times. And I heard Roland Kirk a whole bunch of times too at the Vanguard. Both of them. And at Slug’s and various other places. And I got to hear a whole lot of other people too. Once I discovered that jazz existed and there I am growing up in New York – my parents never listened to jazz. My dad is actually a singer. He’s 102, he’s still alive. And my mom is 99. And they love the Metropolitan Opera and Broadway and all this classical stuff. They might have had a Benny Goodman album and they had maybe a Louis Armstrong album. But I never heard jazz in the house, even though I was an improviser. You know like I had the jazz spirit but I didn’t know what the music really was. And then once I discovered what the music was I thought oh I feel at home here. This is what I want to do you know. I want to do this and how do I learn how to do this? So this band that I had with a bunch of friends, we evolved through all these different styles and then we started playing jazz together and I started writing my own tunes before I knew standards. You know I didn’t come about it in any kind of orthodox way. And then when I went to Northwestern – which is how I ended up out here – I auditioned for the jazz band. And they did not have a jazz department back then, but they had a jazz band. And I wasn’t in the music school but I really wanted to do this. So all the other guys were all veterans of high school jazz programs, which the school I went to didn’t have a jazz program of any sort. And so I auditioned and I could swing, you know when I was eighteen. I had this feel and I could play over changes to a certain extent you know, and so I got the gig. And the band was led by Bunky Green.
